title: Chapter 124 – Sang Ruo's Last Lesson
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Elder Ye]

Nineteen days later.

Ye has taught the oldest script to four hundred and eleven pupils, and she has never once been the pupil in her own classroom.

She is the pupil now. She sits on a low stool at the foot of a narrow bed in the back room of the Sutra Hall, with a slate on her knee and a stub of chalk in her hand, and her teacher lies propped on three pillows in the thin gray light of early morning and corrects her handwriting. The window is open a hand's breadth. The smell of ink and old paper comes through it from the stacks, together with the first cold wind of autumn.

"Again," says Sang Ruo.

Ye writes the character a second time. It is a single stroke, a hooked line like a fishing barb, and it means remain. It is the fourth word in the Founders' first sentence. She has written it perhaps ten thousand times.

"Your wrist is stiff."

"My wrist is seventy-nine years old."

"Mine is a hundred and twelve." The dry voice is almost cheerful. "I do not accept excuses from people who are younger than me. Soften it. Let the hook come from the shoulder, not the hand."

Ye softens it. The chalk squeaks. The line comes out clean, with a small flick at the end, like a bird lifting off a branch.

"Better," says her teacher. "You have not forgotten everything."

"I have forgotten most of it."

"Of course you have. It is why I am teaching it." Sang Ruo shifts on the pillows with a small, careful breath. She is thinner than she was three weeks ago. Her hands, on the gray blanket, are as light and spotted as dead leaves. But her eyes are bright. "I did not have you for thirty years in order to be remembered. I had you in order that someone should know how to read."

* * *

The lessons are all she asks for, and Ye gives her every hour she can steal.

There is the Sutra Hall to run, and the Council to attend, and the endless dull business of the Sect, which has acquired in the weeks since the Offering a feverish intensity, as though a man who had been starved were trying to eat at a feast. Ye sits through it with her stick between her knees and her face blank. At noon she goes to the back room. At dusk she returns. At night she sleeps in the chair by the bed, in her robe, with her head against the wall.

She has not told anyone what the lessons are for. She is not entirely sure herself.

On the sixth day, Sang Ruo had her write out the first page of the Roll of Keepers from memory. On the ninth, the oldest hymn of the Gate. On the twelfth, a long list of plain words that had no connection to one another: door, ash, tide, root, hollow, seam. Ye had written them one by one, and when she asked what they meant, her teacher had only smiled and said, You will know it when you need it. A good key does not announce its lock.

Now, on the nineteenth day, the old woman lies with her eyes closed and her mouth moving, and Ye knows, quite suddenly, with the certainty of a bell striking, that this is the last.

"Teacher," she says.

"Hush." Sang Ruo opens her eyes. "Fetch the stick."

* * *

The Council meets at ten, and Ye attends it the way a woman attends her own trial.

Qin Hao sits at the foot of the long table, where the Gate Elder has always sat, with his hands flat on the wood in front of him. They are not hands any longer. Since the night of the Registry's strike they are two blocks of gray stone from the wrist down, smooth and heavy, and he has learned to turn a page with the edge of one. Nobody at the table looks at them. Everybody knows exactly where they are.

"The Treasury reports a shortfall," says Elder Zhou's replacement, a nervous man with ink on his cuff. "Eleven hundred stones against the quarter."

"The Treasury reports a shortfall every quarter," says Qin Hao. "This is the first one that has a name attached."

"Whose name?"

"Yours, if you do not find the stones by the new moon."

The man goes white. Ye lets it pass. She has watched this Council grow teeth in the weeks since the Offering, and she is not sure she likes the look of them, but they are better teeth than the ones it had before. A year ago these men would have smiled and voted for whichever way the wind blew from the Cloud Peak. Now they argue. They argue badly and loudly, and sometimes they are right.

When the meeting breaks, Qin Hao catches her at the door. He does not touch her; he cannot, without care. He stands a pace away and lowers his voice.

"How is she?"

"Dying."

"I know. I am asking how she is."

Ye considers the question. It is the first time in a month that anyone has asked it correctly.

"She is correcting my handwriting," she says.

Something shifts in the stone-gray face, something that is almost a smile. "Then she is well. Tell her the Gate stair is clean. Tell her no one has crossed it since the wall went up." He hesitates. "Tell her I said the word, once, at night, when I was alone. The one from the old tablets. I think it is a name. I think it is Cole."

"Do not say it again."

"I have not." His eyes are steady. "But it says itself, sometimes, in my sleep."

She promises to carry the message. She does not tell him she will also carry the warning.

* * *

Wenyuan comes at dusk, with Yue at his side and Pebble padding between them.

They do not come into the back room. Ye meets them in the passage, under the lamp, and the four of them stand there awkwardly like people at a gate. Wenyuan, at sixty-three, is a broad, quiet man with a farmer's shoulders and a Foundation Establishment cultivator's stillness, and he turns his cap in his hands. Yue wears a plain gray robe and a bandage on her left ear, because she has been listening too hard again.

"We will not stay," Wenyuan says. "We only wished you to know that the clan has set a lamp in the Garden Hall for her. It will burn until she is gone."

"The clan," Ye repeats.

"Three hundred and ninety-six. Every one of them has put a hand on the lamp." He looks down at his cap. "My son says she held a wall for him for thirty-five years. In my house, a debt like that is not paid. It is carried."

Ye looks at the big, shy man, and finds that she has nothing at all to say.

Pebble lifts her small gray head and fixes her eyes on the door of the back room. She does not growl. She does not move. She only says, in her clear child's voice, the first sentence that Ye has ever heard from her.

"She is not afraid."

Yue goes pale. "She does that," she whispers. "She hears the seams, and then she says what is in them."

"What is in this one?" asks Ye.

The little beast considers. "A very long stairway," says Pebble. "And a woman, at the bottom, who has already put down the lamp."

Nobody speaks. Wenyuan bows to Ye, a farmer's bow, low and plain, and takes his daughter's arm, and they go away down the stair together. The lamp throws their three shadows long on the wall, and the smallest, for a moment, looks like a woman holding a book.

* * *

Jian comes in the last hour of the afternoon, and he does not stay.

He stands in the doorway of the back room in his plain gray cloak with his hood down, thirty-six years old and looking older, with the drawn, careful face of a man who has recently paid a debt in a coin he does not like to name. He does not speak. He looks at the old woman on the pillows, and she looks at him, and a long, level, unembarrassed silence passes between them.

"You came," says Sang Ruo.

"I came to say thank you."

"You said it already, in your way, when you opened the door." Her smile is faint. "I felt it. A Keeper feels what happens in her House. You went in and you came out, and you left a piece of yourself in the dark, and you did not complain."

Jian says nothing. His right hand closes slowly, and opens.

"What did it take?" she asks.

"A name."

"Which?"

"My mother used to call me something. When I was small." He says it flatly, as a man reports a stolen purse. "I cannot remember what."

The old woman's eyes close. When they open they are wet. "I am sorry," she says. "It is a cruel house. It takes the small things first, because they are the ones you will not miss until you reach for them."

"I will manage."

"You will. That is the trouble with you." The thin hand lifts a little from the blanket. "Boy. Whatever is coming, whatever you do with the rest of the door, do not do it alone. Do you hear me? I have watched thirty-one Keepers die alone, and I was one of them. It is not a good way to go."

He bows, very low, and does not trust himself to answer. When he straightens, his eyes are red and perfectly dry. He turns and goes away down the stair, and Ye listens to his steps until they are gone, and then she looks at her teacher.

"What did he mean?" she asks. "About the name?"

"He meant that he is already paying," says Sang Ruo. "And that he does not know yet how much."

* * *

It leans against the wall by the door, where it has leaned for nineteen days.

Ye has carried it for fifty-five years. She received it in the winter of the year four hundred and forty-one, in a cold anteroom of the Sutra Hall, from a clerk who said only that the Master left this for you. A plain length of black wood, knotted at the head and shod with iron at the foot, no longer than the distance from her hip to the floor. She had thought it a walking-stick. She had worn a groove in the grain of it with her thumb.

She carries it to the bed and lays it across the blanket.

Sang Ruo's hand finds it, by touch, without opening her eyes. Her fingers move along the wood to the iron ferrule at the foot. They close round it. And with a small, practiced twist, as though she had done it a thousand times, she turns it a quarter and draws.

The stick opens.

It does not break. It unscrews, at the hidden seam an inch above the iron, and the lower section comes away in her hand like a cork from a bottle. Inside, where the wood should be solid, there is a hollow. And in the hollow, rolled tight as a pencil and no thicker than a finger, lies a scroll of plum-colored paper.

Ye does not move. She cannot.

"Fifty-five years," she says at last. Her voice sounds like someone else's. "I oiled it every spring."

"I know. I hoped you would." The old woman's smile is warm and tired. "A hollow takes oil badly. It would have told you if you had looked."

"I did not look."

"You never did." She draws out the scroll with two fingers and lays it in Ye's lap. "That is why I gave it to you."

* * *

It is a list of names.

Ye unrolls it with fingers that tremble. It runs the whole length of the paper, a hand's breadth wide and nearly an arm's length long, closely written in a tiny, upright, patient script, in plum ink. There are no titles. There are no numbers. There are only names, one beneath another, hundreds of them, each with a date beside it. She reads the first. Then the second. Then a third, and her heart gives a hard, slow knock, because she knows the third.

Pei Wanli. Hall of Weights. Burned in the year 488.

"These are the names," says Sang Ruo quietly. "The ones they burned. Every Number who ever gave up a name to the House, from the first year of my keeping to the last. I copied them, one by one, each night after the burning, by candle, in a closet at the back of the ridge-house. It took me twenty-two years to get the habit, and thirty-three to keep it. The House never knew."

"A Keeper is not supposed to—"

"A Keeper is supposed to forget." The thin voice is dry as dust. "I forgot nothing. It is the one sin I am proud of."

Ye looks down at the paper. Four hundred and some lines. In the margin of each, in a smaller hand, a second note: a family, a town, a trade, a nickname. Pei Wanli, who sang while he worked. Chen Dao, left-handed. Su Ming, afraid of dogs. Beside the last, written in a hand that shakes: Mu Daoren, who chose.

"When a name is burned," says Sang Ruo, "the Number forgets it. Not at once. Over a year, it slips, like water out of a cracked jar. By the time he has served five years he cannot say it aloud. By ten he has stopped hearing it in dreams. The House keeps them by this. A man who has lost his name cannot leave; he has nowhere to go."

"And with the list—"

"With the list, he can be called by it." The pale eyes meet hers. "Read a name aloud to its owner. Read it in the oldest script, in a voice he trusts. He will remember. It does not undo the burning. But it gives him back the one thing the House took, and a man who has his own name back is not a Number any longer."

Ye is utterly still. The scroll lies in her lap like a live coal.

"Forty-one in this Sect," she says. "Four thousand in the world."

"Four thousand and some. It is all there." Sang Ruo's breath catches. "I could not read them. Not aloud. The Keeper's voice is bound; a Keeper who speaks a burned name is struck down. I had to wait. I had to find someone who could."

"Someone who was not a Keeper."

"Someone who had been loved." The old woman's hand finds Ye's, and holds it. "I could think of only one."

* * *

Qinghe brings soup at noon, and nobody stops her.

She comes up the narrow stair of the Sutra Hall's back wing with a covered bowl in both hands, a small woman in a brown shawl, and stands in the doorway for a moment, looking at the bed. She does not fuss. She has seen death before, in her own house and her neighbors', and she knows it has a smell, and a quiet, and a way of making the air stand still. She crosses the room and sets the bowl on the sill.

"Ginger and chicken," she says. "Nothing heavy."

"You are kind," says Sang Ruo.

"I am practical. A person who is leaving should not leave hungry." Qinghe sits on the edge of the stool beside Ye, without being asked, and takes the old woman's hand between her own. "I have come to say thank you."

"For what?"

"For my son." Her voice is steady. "You gave him a wall when he needed one. You kept him alive in the dark when you could have let the House have him. I do not know what you did or how, but I know that for thirty-five years a woman I never met has been standing between my boy and a very great harm." She presses the thin fingers. "I wished you to hear it said."

Sang Ruo does not answer at once. A tear rolls slowly down her cheek, and she does not wipe it away.

"I was afraid I had done wrong," she says. "I was afraid that to keep him I had made him a captive."

"You made him a child with a mother," says Qinghe. "That is all anyone can do."

She stays an hour. She feeds the old woman soup from a spoon, a mouthful at a time, and wipes her chin with her apron, and talks of the Garden, and the silver-thread, and Hu's new forge, and the ridiculous opinions of a pangolin. When she rises to go, Sang Ruo is asleep, and Qinghe lays the blanket straight over her feet and looks at Ye across the bed.

"She loves you," she says, very quietly. "More than she has ever known how to say."

Ye does not answer at once. She follows Qinghe to the head of the stair instead, and watches the small figure descend with one hand on the rail, slowly, favoring her left knee. Sixty-one years old, Qi Refining Six, with perhaps forty years left and a husband she has insisted must go first. Ye has spent three decades among people who counted their remaining years like misers. This woman counts hers like a housewife counting eggs, and spends them just as freely.

When the small figure is gone, Ye goes back inside, and she sits for a long time with the soup going cold on the sill and the scroll in her hand.

* * *

It is evening when Sang Ruo wakes, and she knows at once what she is going to do.

Ye sees it in her face. She sees it in the way the old woman's eyes clear, and her mouth firms, and her thin hands push at the blanket. She sees it in the way the light lies on her cheek, soft and gold and final, the last light of an autumn day. She puts out a hand.

"Teacher. No."

"Child." The voice is a thread, but it is steady. "You know what I am for."

"You are not for anything. You are my teacher."

"I am the thirty-first Keeper of the Roll, and for fifty-five years I have been a hinge on which a door swung the wrong way." Sang Ruo's smile is sweet and terrible. "There is one line left in the Roll. Did you know? One. A single blank line, at the foot of the last page. When a Keeper dies, the Roll writes the name of the next."

"Writes it itself?"

"By will. By the will of the House, that has no one to hold it now but the habit of six centuries." The old woman's eyes close. "It will name someone. I do not know whom. It may name a Number. It may name one of the sleepers. It may name your Operator, because he is the eighth, and the House has waited for the eighth. And whoever it names will sit in my chair and wear my veil and learn the whole of what I learned, and I will have died for nothing."

"Then stay alive."

"I cannot. I have days. Perhaps hours." The thin hand tightens on hers. "But I have one thing I can still do. A Keeper may burn her own name from the Roll. Not as a Number does, to serve. As a Keeper does, to close. It is the last act of the office. The first Keeper wrote it into the Rule, in case the House ever needed to be ended. No one has done it. It costs the one who does it everything she has."

"Everything."

"Her breath." Sang Ruo almost laughs. "I would have it anyway."

Ye cannot speak.

"If I burn it now, while I am the Keeper, the line closes. There is no successor. The Roll cannot write a thirty-second name, because there is no thirty-first left to hand it on." The pale eyes open and fix on Ye's face. "The House does not die. But it loses its mouth. It cannot choose. It cannot speak. It can only hold what it has."

"And the names?"

"Are yours." She presses the scroll into Ye's palm. "The only part of the Roll that I could take with me. Read them. One by one. Take as long as you need. They will not all come home, child. Some are too far gone. But some will."

The light is going out of the window. The wind in the stacks has dropped. In the garden below, very far away, a child is calling another across the dusk.

"I do not know how to do this," says Ye.

"You have never needed to know how." The old woman's voice is soft. "Only to be willing."

* * *

She dies at the turn of the watch, with her pupil's hand in hers.

There is no ceremony. There is no sound. Sang Ruo lays her left palm flat on the blanket, where the old plum-colored Roll lies, a worn heavy book with a cloth cover, and she speaks a single word in the oldest script. Ye knows it. It is the hooked character. Remain. The old woman says it clearly, as to a child learning a lesson. And the book on the blanket shivers, and a thin line of plum-colored light runs down the edge of its last page, and a name that has been written there for fifty-five years begins, very slowly, to fade.

Sang Ruo.

It goes. Letter by letter. The ink thins, and pales, and is gone, and where it was the paper lies blank and clean and cold. The old woman's hand goes limp. Her breath stops in the middle of a sentence. And on her face, Ye sees, there is an expression she has never seen on it in all their years: peace. Not triumph. Not relief. The peace of a very tired person who has put down a very heavy thing and found that her arms still work.

Ye sits there for a long time.

She holds the thin cooling fingers. She says nothing. She does not weep; she is not, she thinks, built for it. But her shoulders shake, once, and she bends and lays her forehead on the blanket by her teacher's hand and stays there until the stub of the candle burns low.

Then she gets up. She folds the dead woman's hands. She draws the blanket over her face, tenderly, with both palms. She takes the stick, and screws it shut, and puts the scroll of names inside her robe against her heart. She goes to the window, and shuts it against the cold.

And on the sill, beside the cold bowl of soup, she sees the Roll.

It is lying open to the last page, where she left it, on the blanket's edge. She had not noticed. She had thought it dead, now. She reaches for it, to close it, and her hand stops an inch above the paper.

On the last line, in fresh plum ink, wet and shining in the candlelight, a new name is being written.

The brush is invisible. The hand is no one's. The characters come slowly, stroke by stroke, in a firm upright script she has never seen, and Ye watches them form one at a time, with the horror of a woman watching a stranger sign her name.

Thirty-second Keeper of the Roll.

Lin Jian.
